title.analysis: Authentic title "POV: Your Life With Every Level of Debt (& What To Do)" uses the social-media "POV" framing with a tiered "every level" structure and a parenthetical promise of action. The script delivers five explicit levels (car, student loans, cards, mortgage, floor drops) through one narrated character. The tier ladder echoes the channel's level/threshold titles. TYPICAL against the cohort; association only, no CTR or experiment evidence.

The recurring cartoon man in a blue hoodie escalates: holding a card and cash (worried); sweating with bills and a chain on one wrist; collapsed in a pile of bills and cards wrapped in red chains, with a curved arrow pointing at him. The escalating triptych matches the title's "every level" structure, though the script follows a female character (Maya) and never uses $5K/$50K/$200K tiers (packaging-content mismatch in specifics). script.opening_words: Two women graduate the same year from the same state university. Same degree, same starting salary, $48,000 marketing coordinator, mid-size city, same rent, same monthly take home of about $3,100 after taxes. Their apartments are 3 miles apart. They get coffee at the same place on Sunday mornings. 10 years later, one of them opens her banking app on a Tuesday and checks her balance the way you'd check the weather, casually, no stakes. She has $47,000 in a brokerage
script.ending_words: and by 55 it was worth $820,000 the system is not going to tell you any of this that's why I'm telling you if this hit close to home drop a comment and tell me which level you're at right now and if you haven't subscribed yet now's the time because there's more math to run and it gets a lot less brutal once you can actually see it coming
script.analysis: Full 19813 canonical characters read. A narrative debt-ladder explainer following "Maya" from 23 to 29: car loan and dealer F&I add-ons, student loans, credit cards and minimum-payment design, an FHA-style 5%-down mortgage with full housing costs, then shocks (water heater, medical bill, reduced hours), bankruptcy statistics, an alternate Maya who invested the car payment, macro cost-vs-income claims, and practical rules. Budget and loan arithmetic largely reproduce (car $499, student loan $386, housing $2,797, -$667 deficit, $2.2M at 8%). Verified: 565,759 bankruptcy filings in 2025 (+11%); card debt ~$1.28T record (implied from NY Fed Q1 2026). Supported with caveat: Stewart (2009) minimum-payment anchoring. Errors: the $3,200 at 24% example ($54/$10 split) is impossible under its own 2% rule; the "+$50" payoff of $3,700 is understated (~$4,660). Unverified or contested: two-thirds medical bankruptcy, 1990-2025 cost increases, $1T interest. Internal inconsistencies: savings vs cash car, card minimums $108 vs $185, 2021 vs 2019 Honda. The final third is unpunctuated ASR. The stored ending is complete.
beat_map: Cold open: two identical graduates diverge after 10 years.
Level 1: car loan, four-square, F&I add-ons; $879 true cost.
Level 2: student loans; $386/month; payoff and balance-growth stats.
Level 3: credit cards; store-card markup; national card debt; minimum-payment math and anchoring study.
Level 4: mortgage at 29; full housing cost $2,797; -$667 budget; workarounds; inspector.
Level 5: shocks, reduced hours, the unopened drawer.
Bankruptcy statistics and medical debt; the automatic stay.
$1,500 debt service at 8% = $2.2M; cost vs income since 1990; $1T interest.
Not a character flaw: structural framing.
Practical rules: total cost, pay above minimum, approval is not affordability.

claim_audit.assessment: K02: 24%/12 x $3,200 = $64 interest, so a pure 2%-of-balance minimum covers interest only and the balance never falls; the $54/$10 split is wrong (it would require ~20% APR). Under the common 1%-plus-interest rule (min $25), payoff takes about 15.9 years, $5,287 interest, $8,487 total -- the video's 14 years / $4,800 / $8,000 is the right order of magnitude but internally inconsistent with its own 2% rule.
